**Course:** 12-week Low Altitude Economics · 2026–27  
**Instructor:** Chiu Yu Ko

**New here?** **Short path:** [What is LAE?](primer.qmd) → this overview → [Week 1](week-01.qmd). The primer explains the field in simple English; this page is the week map. **Full Orient** (business, regulators, HowTo, FAQ, Key numbers) is on [How to use this site](howto.qmd#full-orient).

Weekly lecture pages sit under **Teach** (for example [Week 1](week-01.qmd)).

## Description

This course is about the **economics and business strategy** of the **low-altitude economy (LAE)**.

LAE means services that use low-altitude airspace — not only the aircraft itself. Vehicle types, sites, traffic labels, and trial programmes are introduced on [What is LAE?](primer.qmd). Formal definitions sit in the [Glossary](glossary.qmd).

- **Where we focus:** Hong Kong and the **Greater Bay Area (GBA)** — the city cluster that includes Hong Kong, Macao, and nearby Guangdong cities.
- **Comparators:** Selected global **advanced air mobility (AAM)** frameworks (ideas for new air services in cities). These are for comparison only. They are **not** Hong Kong law. See Objectives below and the week pages under **Teach**.
- **What you practise:** Turn use cases into demand, unit economics, infrastructure breakeven, partnerships, regulatory roadmaps, airspace choices, sustainability, risk, and investment recommendations.
- **How weeks work:** Each week adds tools (cost and demand measures, competition checks, infrastructure and partnership logic, and related methods). Names and formulas appear on each week page when you need them. This page does not list every acronym.
- **Capstone:** Combine those tools into one clear business or policy strategy for a Hong Kong / GBA service that can work commercially, be accepted socially, fit policy, and scale.

## Objectives

- Learn the economics and business strategy of LAE in Hong Kong and the GBA, with global AAM examples for comparison only.
- Practise tools for demand, unit economics, sites, partnerships, regulation, airspace, sustainability, and risk.
- Put those tools together into one business or policy strategy (capstone) and into exam answers.

## Learning outcomes

After this course, you should be able to:

- Explain demand and supply for **urban air mobility** (city air services) in Hong Kong and the GBA, using simple economic tools and who is affected.
- Size a market and judge an investment with basic cost–benefit thinking — without mixing revenue, value added, and social benefit.
- Discuss pricing, incentives, and congestion rules that support sustainability and public acceptance.
- Map value-chain roles and the economics of regulation, using selected global cases (for example NASA, McKinsey, AiRMOUR) for comparison — not as Hong Kong law.
- Build a clear business or policy strategy through scenarios and team work (capstone).
